newsitem.title: USA: World Bank stepping up support for Russia.
newsitem.headline: World Bank stepping up support for Russia.

text.p: The World Bank, sensing an economic turnaround in Russia is at hand, is significantly stepping up support for the country, bank officials said Friday.

"Russia is at the crossroads of its economic reform programme," World Bank Vice President Johannes Linn told reporters. "We have a tremendous window of opportunity to help accelerate Russia's economic recovery."

The lending agency said its board approved nearly $885 million in loans for Russia on Thursday. The biggest credit -- a $600 million structural adjustment loan -- will help Russia overhaul and stabilise its economy.

The bank, which makes development loans, is expected to approve another $800 million credit by the end of this month as part of a programme to lend Russia up to $6 billion in 1997-98. If fully carried out, the programme would nearly double the bank's assistance to Russia.
Linn acknowledged that there were risks involved in the stepped-up lending programme, but he argued that now was the time for the bank to boost its support of Russia's reforms.
"The turnaround is just about here," he said.

The bank is looking for Russia's economy to grow about 4 percent next year and 6 percent annually thereafter, after stagnating this year. Foreign direct investment is also expected to pick up, to $2.5 billion this year and as much as $3 billion in 1998, from $2 billion in 1996, officials said.
"There is a resurgence of private-sector interest and confidence in Russia at this juncture," Linn said.
Besides the $600 million structural adjustment loan, the other bank credits approved for Russia were:
-- $85 million to help recently privatised companies restructure;
-- $66 million for health care reform, including improved outpatient care;
-- $40 million to reform the problem-plagued power sector;
-- $22.6 million to improve government analysis of the economy.

Linn said Russia received broad-based support for its "ambitious" reform programme from other countries at the bank board meeting Thursday. But some areas of concern were cited, including Moscow's still-difficult budgetary position.

Russia is also making better use of the $6.4 billion in loans that the bank had previously approved for the country, officials said. Dispersal of some of those loans had been slow, in part because of Russia's unfamiliarity with bank procedures, but has picked up significantly.
